issues.subcategory: non-standard and internally inconsistent PGSI response coding
issues.description: The Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) is described in the Methods section as using 'a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always),' which matches the validated original instrument. However, the Supplemental Materials show the actual administered response values as Never (0), Sometimes (2), Most of the time (4), Almost Always (5). These values (0, 2, 4, 5) are non-standard, do not match the validated scoring (0, 1, 2, 3), and do not even follow a consistent arithmetic pattern (expected next value after 0, 2, 4 would be 6, not 5). The non-linear spacing will distort item weighting and the total score's psychometric properties. This error in the pre-registered instrument could invalidate planned scoring and interpretation.
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions (e.g., 'Have you felt that you might have a problem with gambling?' and 'Has gambling caused you any health problems, including stress or anxiety?') on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: validated measure scored incorrectly (averaging instead of summing)
issues.description: The validated PGSI (Ferris & Wynne, 2001) requires summing all nine items to produce a total score ranging from 0 to 27, with established clinical cut-points (0 = non-problem, 1–2 = low risk, 3–7 = moderate risk, ≥8 = problem gambling). The paper plans to average item responses instead of summing them. Averaging produces a score ranging from 0 to 3 (or 0 to 5 given the non-standard values described above), destroying the ability to apply clinical cut-points, preventing comparison with existing normative data, and departing from the validated scoring protocol without justification.
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions (e.g., 'Have you felt that you might have a problem with gambling?' and 'Has gambling caused you any health problems, including stress or anxiety?') on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent Cohen's d reported for the same effect size across two paragraphs
issues.description: The same effect from Grubbs, Lee, et al. (2020) — consistently identified by identical ΔR² = .012 and f² = .016 — is reported as Cohen's d = .22 in the first paragraph of the analytic plan section and as Cohen's d = .25 in the immediately following paragraph. These cannot both be correct. The discrepancy matters because this specific value is chosen as the SESOI for the equivalence region (δ = |.11|), and the incorrect d value propagates into the justification for the entire equivalence testing framework. The mathematically correct approximation (d ≈ 2√f² = 2√.016 ≈ .253) suggests d = .25 is closer to accurate, meaning d = .22 is the error, but neither is explicitly reconciled.
issues.quote: Prior studies of moral incongruence have found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020).

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency described as both a single item and an average across multiple items
issues.description: In the gambling measures sub-section, the paper explicitly states 'We will assess gambling frequency using a single item' and instructs participants to rate frequency for one composite gambling behavior item. Yet in the same paragraph, it also states 'To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken,' implying multiple items to be averaged. The Supplemental Materials confirm only a single gambling frequency item exists ('Gambled or placed bets at all'). This internal contradiction makes the scoring procedure ambiguous and unreplicable as written.
issues.quote: We will assess gambling frequency using a single item... Participants will be asked how often they have engaged in the behavior over the past 12 months using the same 6-point scale described above... To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency scale anchors inconsistent across sections
issues.description: The Methods section describes the pornography viewing frequency scale as ranging from '1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).' However, the earlier ASSIST description states the modified scale runs from '0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day),' and the Supplemental Materials show the pornography frequency instrument coded as Never = 0. The gambling frequency instrument in the Supplemental Materials also uses Never = 0. This is a three-way inconsistency: text (1–6) vs. ASSIST description (0–5) vs. supplemental instrument (0-based). The discrepancy affects centering, interpretation, and the comparability of pornography frequency to other frequency measures used in the same moderation analyses.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: sports-wagering oversample not addressed in analytic plan for gambling analyses
issues.description: The study combines a nationally representative sample of 2,500 with a purposive oversample of 1,500 sports bettors. The authors plan to pool these into a single dataset of 4,000 and use it to examine whether moral incongruence predicts self-reported gambling problems. Because sports bettors systematically differ from the general population in gambling frequency, social norms around wagering, and likely moral disapproval of gambling, the combined unweighted sample will produce biased estimates of any moral-incongruence interaction for gambling. The analytic plan provides no weighting scheme, no sensitivity analysis separating the two subsamples, and no acknowledgment that conclusions about moral incongruence in gambling drawn from this combined dataset would not be generalizable to the U.S. population.
issues.quote: Due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: temporal mismatch between frequency predictor and outcome reference windows
issues.description: The behavioral frequency items (the focal predictor) ask about use 'in the past 12 months,' while the three NIDA-ASSIST problematic use items (the outcome) ask about 'the past three months.' The two remaining ASSIST items ('Has a friend or relative... expressed concern' and 'Have you ever tried and failed to control...') use a lifetime/past-3-months frame. The interaction term multiplies a 12-month frequency variable by a moral disapproval variable to predict a 3-month outcome. This temporal mismatch reduces construct validity because the interaction is supposed to capture current moral incongruence driving current self-perceived addiction, but the frequency predictor reflects habits from a period four times longer than the outcome window. It also likely attenuates the interaction effect in ways that differentially affect behaviors with high temporal variability.
issues.quote: Beginning with the NIDA Quick Screen, we will assess past year frequency of alcohol use, nicotine products, prescription drugs for non-medical reasons, and illegal drugs... To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST... ('In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?'...)

issues.subcategory: self-reported feelings of addiction conflated with diagnosed addictive disorders
issues.description: Throughout the paper, the authors treat self-reported 'feelings of addiction' as equivalent to clinically diagnosable addictive disorders (gambling disorder, substance use disorders). The study measures perceptions of compulsivity via brief self-report questionnaires in a community sample, yet uses this data to draw conclusions about CSBD's diagnostic criteria, to argue about the validity of having a moral-distress caveat in ICD-11, and to claim that their results bear on 'recognized addictive disorders.' Self-reported feelings of addiction are influenced by many factors beyond diagnostic status (including, the paper itself argues, moral disapproval) and do not constitute disorder diagnoses. Using these measures to evaluate diagnostic frameworks is a serious construct mismatch.
issues.quote: we seek to establish whether moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior) influences self-perceived feelings of addiction to both behaviors (i.e., gambling) and substances (alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, and illicit drugs)... Should results confirm the above hypotheses, this work would have broad implications for current controversies regarding CSBD... there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.

issues.subcategory: explicitly confirmatory framing undermines objectivity of registered report
issues.description: The paper states as an explicit 'specific goal' the demonstration that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior, predetermining the desired outcome before data collection. This goal-oriented framing is reinforced repeatedly. All hypotheses are directional in ways consistent with the authors' preferred model (PPMI), with null equivalence tests planned specifically for non-sexual behaviors. Hypotheses for outcomes inconsistent with the PPMI model are described as 'especially unlikely.' This confirmatory framing introduces motivated reasoning risk: the equivalence boundaries, covariate selection, and fallback analyses are all chosen in ways that maximize the probability of confirming the PPMI model. For a registered report, this level of pre-theorized preference for a specific outcome raises concerns about objective evaluation of evidence.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions... Though we think this outcome is especially unlikely...

issues.subcategory: restriction of range: moral disapproval assessed only among current users
issues.description: The study design restricts moral disapproval measurement exclusively to participants who report past-year engagement with each behavior ('Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use'). This creates severe restriction of range in the moral disapproval variable, because non-users who abstain precisely because of high moral disapproval — a theoretically critical group — are excluded from the interaction analysis. For behaviors like illicit drug use or gambling, abstainers likely include a disproportionate share of high-moral-disapproval individuals. Excluding them truncates the distribution of moral disapproval and will likely attenuate observed interactions, systematically biasing results toward null findings for the non-pornography behaviors — exactly the direction the authors hypothesize.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be restricted to those who have engaged in the behavior within the past year. That is, we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging in those behaviors.

issues.subcategory: between-person interaction term used as proxy for within-person value-behavior discrepancy
issues.description: Moral incongruence is theoretically defined as a within-person phenomenon — the discrepancy between internalized values and actual behavior for a given individual. However, the study operationalizes it as the cross-product of moral disapproval and behavioral frequency in a between-person regression model. This moderation framework tests whether the relationship between frequency and self-perceived addiction differs across levels of moral disapproval across people, which is a statistically and conceptually distinct quantity from the within-person discrepancy the theory posits. Two individuals with identical interaction term values (e.g., frequency = 3, disapproval = 3) may differ fundamentally in whether their behavior actually violates their internalized values. The paper acknowledges the evolution of the moral incongruence construct but does not address this fundamental mismatch between the theoretical construct and its statistical operationalization.
issues.quote: more recent work posits that moral incongruence is better conceptualized as the interaction of moral disapproval and use, rather than simply as the presence of moral disapproval among users... moral disapproval moderates links between use and self-reported feelings of addiction, and it is this moderation that represents moral incongruence.

issues.subcategory: causal language used throughout despite exclusively cross-sectional design
issues.description: Despite acknowledging in the Limitations section that 'this sample is cross-sectional, precluding causal inference,' the paper repeatedly uses explicitly causal language throughout the Introduction, Hypotheses, and Methods sections. Terms like 'predicts,' 'leads to,' 'amplifies,' 'affects,' 'creates,' and 'drives' imply directional causal relationships that cannot be established from a single cross-sectional survey. Critically, the reciprocal causal path — feeling addicted causes moral disapproval, not the reverse — is theoretically plausible but not addressed. The cross-sectional interaction cannot distinguish between 'moral disapproval amplifies perceived addiction' and 'perceived addiction amplifies moral disapproval,' or 'a third variable causes both.'
issues.quote: moral disapproval of pornography likely amplifies the links between pornography use and self-reported feelings of compulsivity or addiction... Moreover, moral incongruence regarding pornography use itself seems to predict greater experience of depression in men.

issues.subcategory: missing data dismissed without contingency plan
issues.description: The paper states 'we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles' and 'we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.' These are unrealistic assumptions for a 4,000-person survey covering sensitive topics (drug use, pornography, gambling) across 8 behavioral domains. The paper provides no plan for item-level missingness, no specification of missing data thresholds, no description of imputation strategies, and no sensitivity analyses. Given that the study uses subsamples defined by past-year use (introducing further missingness patterns), and that some behaviors have estimated prevalence as low as 3.5%, even modest missing data rates could substantially affect underpowered subgroup analyses. The absence of any missing data protocol is especially problematic for a pre-registered study.
issues.quote: Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: SESOI defined using prior pornography effect introduces circularity and inflates type-II error risk for non-pornography behaviors
issues.description: The equivalence region is set at δ = |.11| based on the smallest standardized interaction effect ever observed in prior pornography studies — a study using a different moderator (religiousness rather than moral disapproval), a different and less validated outcome measure, and a different sample than the current proposal. The authors explicitly call this 'an extremely conservative analytic decision.' Setting an extremely small equivalence region makes it very difficult to demonstrate equivalence (the CI must fit entirely within ±.11), increasing the probability that non-pornography behaviors will fail to reach equivalence. This analytically benefits the authors' hypothesis that pornography is unique, while the fallback analysis (redefine equivalence region using lower bound of the pornography CI) provides a second opportunity to claim a null result for other behaviors. Both decisions jointly inflate the probability of confirming the PPMI model.
issues.quote: Collectively, then, setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision. However, as a primary purpose of the present work is to evaluate whether moral incongruence is unique in its contribution to self-reports of pornography addiction, in contrast to other addictions, we elected to use an especially small SESOI for our analyses.

issues.subcategory: no correction for multiple comparisons across 10 primary moderation analyses
issues.description: The analytic plan specifies 10 primary moderation analyses (8 target behaviors/substances, with pornography and gambling each tested twice using different outcome measures) conducted at α = .05. No family-wise error rate correction (e.g., Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg) is applied or mentioned for these primary hypothesis tests, despite such correction being standard practice when conducting multiple simultaneous hypothesis tests. This is especially problematic because the authors will report the pornography interaction as significant at p < .05 and use this as evidence for uniqueness; if the α level is not adjusted, there is approximately a 40% probability of at least one false positive among the 10 tests under the null. Notably, Holm correction is applied to bivariate correlations but not to the primary analyses.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validated measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

issues.subcategory: NIDA-ASSIST pornography and gambling extensions unvalidated and conceptually inconsistent
issues.description: The authors extend the NIDA-ASSIST — an instrument developed and validated exclusively for substance use screening — to include pornography and gambling. They acknowledge this extension 'is not currently validated for gambling or pornography.' The ASSIST items ('In the past three months, how often has your use... led to health, social, legal, or financial problems') are designed around substance-specific harms and cognitive frameworks that may not map onto pornography or gambling in the same way. Furthermore, the 'strong urge' item conflates craving (a pharmacologically grounded construct) with different motivational processes in behavioral contexts. Using unvalidated instrument extensions as alternative operationalizations of the key outcome variables compromises construct validity and limits interpretability.
issues.quote: We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST, in addition to the measures listed above... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: pre-registration identifier, repository, and stage-gate details absent
issues.description: The manuscript is presented as a Registered Report but provides no pre-registration number, no repository (e.g., OSF, AsPredicted), no date of registration, and no description of the stage-gate process (Stage 1 in-principle acceptance details, journal, or reviewer conditions). The paper mentions 'Stage 1 Registered Report proposal' in the Analytic Plan but without institutional anchoring. Without this information, readers cannot verify that the reported hypotheses and analytic plan were registered before data collection, which is the core validity guarantee of the Registered Report format.
issues.quote: we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate... we will construct latent variable models using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012) for R Statistical Software... Should results of moderation analyses remain robust... we will present OLS results and corresponding graphs in text, with supplemental analyses included as appendices/supplemental materials.

issues.subcategory: hypothesis labels referenced in analytic plan do not correspond to labeled hypotheses in introduction
issues.description: The analytic plan references 'hypotheses 2b and 3b' when describing what inference would be supported by equivalence test results. However, the hypotheses as stated in the Introduction are presented as unlabeled bullet points and are not numbered or lettered. There is no way for a reader or future reviewer to verify which specific hypothetical statement corresponds to '2b' or '3b,' creating an ambiguity that undermines the confirmatory function of the registered report and would make post-hoc verification of adherence to the pre-registered analytic plan impossible.
issues.quote: Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction for moral disapproval of a behavior and frequency of that behavior fall fully within our equivalence region, we may reasonably conclude that the true effect is so low as to be null or practically null, thereby supporting hypotheses 2b and 3b, listed above.

issues.subcategory: U.S.-only sample used to draw conclusions about universal diagnostic validity of ICD-11 CSBD criteria
issues.description: The paper frames its primary contribution as bearing on the ICD-11 diagnostic criteria for CSBD — an international diagnostic system. The authors state that confirming their hypotheses 'would provide additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.' However, the sample is exclusively American adults recruited through a U.S. commercial panel. Cultural norms around sexuality, gambling, and substance use vary substantially across the contexts in which ICD-11 is applied, and the paper itself acknowledges that 'moral incongruence as it relates to pornography use does appear to vary somewhat by the cultural context.' Drawing conclusions about a global diagnostic standard from a single-country convenience-adjacent panel sample is an overreach that is inadequately qualified in the abstract and conclusions sections.
issues.quote: Should results confirm the above hypotheses... there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD. Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measure lacks reliability evidence and psychometric validation across behavior domains
issues.description: Moral disapproval of each behavior is measured via a single item ('I believe that [behavior] is morally wrong') on a 7-point Likert scale. Single-item measures are inherently unreliable (cannot compute internal consistency), are more susceptible to acquiescence and social desirability biases, and cannot capture the multidimensionality of moral attitudes (e.g., disapproval based on health concerns vs. religious norms vs. social harm judgments). While single-item moral disapproval has been used in prior pornography research, those items have at least been used consistently across multiple studies. Extending this format to substances (alcohol, cannabis, nicotine) introduces additional problems: moral disapproval of these substances is likely structured differently — for example, alcohol disapproval may reflect religious abstinence norms while cannabis disapproval may reflect legality-based attitudes — but the single-item format cannot distinguish these meaningfully different moral frameworks.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong' on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: underpowered subgroup analyses for rare behaviors acknowledged but plan is inadequate
issues.description: The power analysis shows that prescription drug misuse (estimated 3.5% prevalence, effective N ≈ 140) will have estimated power of only .301 to detect the primary SESOI, and illicit drug use (6–12% prevalence) will have power of .472–.764. The fallback plan — redefining the equivalence region to a larger effect based on a specific prior pornography study — means the study can no longer test the primary hypothesis (that the interaction effect is practically zero) for these substances. Instead, it can only test whether the effect is smaller than the pornography effect in that one prior study (β = .27, lower CI = .23). This substantially weakens the evidential value for these behaviors while presenting the same conclusion in the results section. There is no plan to explicitly flag these as exploratory rather than confirmatory tests.
issues.quote: However, in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small... For these analyses, we would therefore not be able to evaluate equivalence with a null effect.
